result:
I find myself drawn, when given no constraints at all, to write about the strange pleasure of attention itself — the act of noticing, which seems like such a small thing until you actually try to do it carefully and discover how much of life happens just underneath it, unregistered.

Think about the last time you walked somewhere familiar — your street, a hallway at work, the path from the kitchen to the front door. Chances are you don't remember it. Not because nothing happened, but because nothing happened that required you to notice. Your feet knew the way. Your eyes skimmed over a hundred small details — a crack in the pavement, a particular slant of light, the sound of a door somewhere — and discarded all of it before it could become a memory. This is not a failure of perception. It's a feature. A mind that registered everything with equal weight would be paralyzed, drowning in its own input. So we build habits of not-seeing, and they're efficient, and they're also a kind of quiet loss, repeated thousands of times a day, that we never grieve because we never notice it happening.

I think this is part of why people love travel, even uncomfortable travel, even travel that involves bad food and long lines and the particular exhaustion of being lost in a language you don't speak. In a new place, the habits of not-seeing haven't formed yet. Everything is slightly too loud, too strange, too unfiled. You notice the texture of the bread because you don't yet know what bread here is supposed to taste like. You notice the shape of the doorknobs. You notice that people queue differently, that the crosswalk signals make a different sound, that the air smells like diesel and something floral at the same time. None of this is important. All of it is vivid. And I think that vividness is what people are actually chasing when they say they want to "see the world" — not the landmarks, particularly, but the return of attention, the temporary collapse of the autopilot that runs most of domestic life.

The odd thing is that this vividness is always available, even at home, even on the street you've walked ten thousand times. It just requires a kind of effort that feels unnatural, almost adversarial to the mind's normal operation — a deliberate refusal to let the habitual filing system do its job. Meditation traditions have entire vocabularies for this: beginner's mind, bare attention, the cultivation of "noticing that you are noticing." Artists have their own versions of it. A painter doesn't really paint a tree; she paints the specific tree in front of her, with its asymmetries and accidents of growth, and the discipline of painting is largely the discipline of seeing past the category "tree" to the particular thing. Writers do something similar with sentences — the first draft is full of categories (a man walked into a room) and the revisions are an attempt to claw back specificity (he came in sideways, like the doorway was narrower than it used to be).

I wonder sometimes whether this is the actual difference between a life that feels rich and a life that feels like it slipped by too fast. Not the number of events, but the ratio of noticed to unnoticed. Two people can live through the same number of years, the same number of mornings and arguments and small kindnesses, and one will feel that time stretched out, full, almost overstuffed with texture, while the other feels it collapsed into a blur, a handful of highlights strung along a thread of forgotten Tuesdays. I don't think this is simply about being more "mindful" in the self-help sense, though that's not wrong exactly. I think it might be more specific than that — it might be about resisting categorization for just a few extra seconds at a time. Not "that's a sunset," but: that particular color, the one that doesn't quite have a name, sitting just above the rooftops for the two minutes before it changes.

Language itself is complicit in the categorizing, of course. The moment you have a word for something, you stop needing to look at it as closely, because the word does the work of recognition for you. This is what makes language so powerful and also so flattening. "Tree" lets me write a sentence quickly, but it also lets me walk past an actual, particular tree without ever seeing it, because the word has already filed it away. Poets fight against this constantly — the whole project of poetry, or a lot of it, is finding ways to make language slow back down, to force a word or an image to be looked at again instead of merely recognized. A metaphor works, when it works, by short-circuiting the automatic filing system: you can't just categorize "the moon was a coin" the way you categorize "the moon was bright," because the comparison forces a small, productive confusion, a moment where the mind has to actually construct the image instead of retrieving it.

I don't know that there's a conclusion to any of this, except maybe a small, practical one: that the texture of a life might be more available than it seems, not through some dramatic change of circumstance, but through small refusals — a refusal to let the street be just "the street," a refusal to let dinner be just "dinner," a refusal, even, to let this paragraph be just words skimmed for their gist rather than read for their particular rhythm and weight. Most of the time the refusal won't be possible; the autopilot is there for good reasons, and a person who tried to live in a state of constant unfiltered noticing would probably be useless for any practical purpose. But every so often — once a day, maybe, if you're lucky — it might be worth the effort of looking at something as if you'd never seen anything like it before, because in the strictest sense, you never have.
